Try every operator as the LAST one applied
The outermost parenthesis splits the expression at exactly one operator
All results of the left and right parts

Substrings repeat across splits; LRU (Least Recently Used) cache without size limit
Descending order as the problem here expects
Results come from different split orders

blocks.h: Why does splitting at the last operator cover every parenthesisation?
p: Any full parenthesisation has one operator applied last, which splits the expression into a left and a right part, each parenthesised independently. Trying every operator as that last one enumerates all of them. Memoising on the substring avoids recomputing the same parts. The number of results is a Catalan number, so the running time is exponential in the output size.

bullets: Time: Exponential: the number of results is a Catalan number.
Space: O(number of results) per memoised substring.

241.takeaway: Divide and conquer: choose each operator as the last applied, combine all left and right results, and memoise substrings.

Peel the tree like an onion
Detach the leaf from its neighbour
A tree has one or two centres

p: Peeling the three leaves leaves only node 1, the only centre.

blocks.h: Why do the centres give minimum height?
p: The height from a root is the distance to its farthest node. The middle of the longest path in a tree is the best root, and a tree has one or two such middle nodes. Peeling leaves layer by layer removes the ends of every long path equally, so what is left is exactly the centre.

310.takeaway: Peel leaf layers until one or two nodes remain: those centres are the roots of minimum-height trees.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Number of bits of the largest value
Only that many bit positions matter
Number x with the lowest `bit` bits removed: its prefix
Set of all prefixes at this level
Is there another prefix q with `p ^ q` equal to the wished prefix `ans | 1`?
Since `p ^ q = c` means `q = c ^ p`
Extend the answer by one bit
Greedy: keep a 1 in this bit if any pair can achieve it

p: A larger XOR is decided by its highest differing bit first, so the best answer takes a 1 in the top bit if any pair allows it, then the next bit, and so on. At each step the question 'can two numbers have prefixes whose XOR equals this wished prefix?' is a lookup in a set of prefixes (a hash version of a binary trie), since a ^ b = c is the same as b = a ^ c.

bullets: Time: O(32·n): one pass over the numbers per bit.
Space: O(n) for the prefix set.

421.takeaway: Greedy on bits from the top: build the answer prefix and test achievability with a set of prefixes (a ^ b = c ⇔ b = a ^ c).

p: `search('hello')` must be False even though the pattern `hell*` exists: the only letter in that bucket is `o`, the query's own letter, so 'changing' it changes nothing. head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Net push on domino i: rightward strength minus leftward strength
Positive → falls right, negative → falls left, zero → stays
Maximum rightward force right after an R
Stronger than any decayed value, since f decays by 1 per cell
Subtracted so the sign tells the winner

p: `.L.R...LR..L..` → `LL.RR.LLRRLL..`:

blocks.h: Why do the forces model the problem?
p: A domino falls toward the NEAREST push that reaches it. Right force at a cell is n minus the distance to the nearest R on its left (if no L is between), and left force is n minus the distance to the nearest L on its right. The larger one wins; equal means the pushes reach it at the same time and cancel. That's why the net sign gives the answer in two linear passes.

838.takeaway: Two passes computing decaying right and left forces; the sign of their difference gives each domino's final state.

State carried from index to index
Extend each previous subarray by x, plus the new subarray `[x]`
Add them to the global set of distinct values

p: OR can only add bits as a subarray grows to the left, so the OR values of subarrays ending at an index form a chain where each value is a superset of the previous one. With at most 30 bits, the chain has at most about 30 distinct values. So each step costs O(30), not O(n), giving O(n·30) instead of O(n²).

bullets: Time: O(n · log(max)): `cur` has at most ~30 distinct values.
Space: O(n · log(max)) for `res` in the worst case.

898.takeaway: Keep the set of ORs of subarrays ending at each index; it stays tiny because OR only adds bits.

p: The judge needs in-degree n−1 and out-degree 0. For anyone else, out-degree ≥ 1 reduces their score, so their in-degree minus out-degree is at most n−2. Only the judge can reach exactly n−1, so one number per person suffices instead of two arrays.

997.takeaway: Degree balance: in-degree minus out-degree equals n − 1 only for the judge.

blocks.h: Why take or skip each word?
p: Each word is either in the chosen set or not, and the choice affects the remaining letter budget for later words. Branching on both options explores all 2ⁿ subsets, but infeasible branches are cut as soon as a word can't be spelled. p: A shared edge connects both Alice and Bob using a single edge, so using it saves one edge relative to adding a type-1 and a type-2 edge for the same link. Taking all useful type-3 edges first, then filling in with single-person edges, minimises the edges kept (a greedy argument like Kruskal's algorithm). head: Code

rows: Number of subarrays containing element i
i+1 choices for the left end, n−i choices for the right end
How many of them have ODD length
Counts alternate odd/even; rounding up covers the case where the total is odd
Contribution of element i to the answer

p: For an element with `a = i+1` choices on the left (including 0 extra elements) and `b = n−i` on the right, a subarray's length is `a' + b' − 1` for chosen `a'` and `b'`. It is odd when `a'` and `b'` have the same parity. The number of such pairs is `ceil(a·b / 2)` when a·b is odd and `a·b / 2` otherwise, which equals `(a·b + 1) // 2` in both cases. This replaces the O(n²) enumeration of subarrays.

1588.takeaway: Contribution counting: element i appears in (i+1)(n−i) subarrays and exactly (that + 1)//2 of them have odd length.

blocks.h: Why preorder and why not delete dead people from the tree?
p: The rule 'person first, then each child's whole family in birth order' is a preorder walk. A dead person's descendants still inherit, so the node must stay in the tree. Marking death in a set (O(1)) is cheaper than restructuring, and the walk simply skips the dead name when printing but still visits their children (as the example shows when `bob` dies).

1600.takeaway: Store the family tree with children lists and a dead set; the order is a preorder traversal that skips dead names but not their descendants.
